issue_context.title: Tessie integration prevents vehicle sleep
issue_context.body:
### The problem

The Tessie integration is polling the Tessie API `https://api.tessie.com/{vin}/state` with use_cache=False. The setting of use_cache=False causes API calls to bypass the Tessie cache and to poll the vehicle directly. This polling prevents vehicle sleep, resulting in continual battery drain and loss of range. Tesla has always strongly recommended against this style of polling. While I understand that with some vehicle models in later releases Tesla has taken some defensive measures to try and mitigate this type of polling behavior, it does not apply to all vehicles, event with 2023.44.30.6 and 2023.44.30.8.

Changing use_cache to True addresses the issue of allowing vehicle sleep, and I am currently running with this.

The setting of use_cache to False appears to have come in just prior to release in order to fix an issue of HA showing vehicle status as awake when it was in fact sleeping. Unfortunately this change completely prevents vehicle sleep. To address the vehicle sleep issue, while still providing vehicle status of sleeping when appropriate, there are a few approaches I have been able to identify.

Approach 1:
Use Tessie's `https://api.tessie.com/{vin}/status` call to separately determine vehicle status ('sleep', 'waiting_for_sleep' or 'awake'), followed by ``https://api.tessie.com/{vin}/state`` (with use_cache=True) to get the rest of the vehicle state. This approach requires two API call per interval, and is the least efficient approach.

Approach 2:
James @ Tessie suggested a simpler approach, which is to use ``https://api.tessie.com/{vin}/state`` (with use_cache=True) to get the current vehicle state, and set the status to sleeping if the vehicle timestamp is older than 60 seconds. This approach has the same number API calls as current, but is inefficient in that it is pulling down the entire vehicle state at all times.

Approach 3:
A variant of approach 1, which is to call `https://api.tessie.com/{vin}/status` call to determine vehicle status, then call ``https://api.tessie.com/{vin}/state`` only if the status has changed state from unknown, 'sleep' or 'waiting_for_sleep' to 'awake'. While this approach is more complex, it would be significantly more efficient in that it would avoid repeatedly pulling the entire vehicle state down when the vehicle is sleeping and it is known that nothing can have changed.

Approach 4:
A slight variant of approach 3, which is to call ``https://api.tessie.com/{vin}/state`` each interval until such time as the vehicle timestamp grows older than 60 seconds, then fall back to just calling `https://api.tessie.com/{vin}/status` until such time as that call returns 'awake'. While a touch more complex that approach 3, this approach is significantly more efficient.

Thoughts?

Appreciate the detailed response. My Model 3 is one of the ones that is able to sleep despite the polling. James and I confirmed this is new behaviour.

Approach 2 from James is against Home Assistant Rules, but Approach 3 seems to be the best immediate fix to me.

I'll work on a PR to add the status API call.

PR rasied, use_cache is always on, and get_state is only called if get_status returns something other than asleep.
I considered turning use_cache off when the vehicle is defintely awake, but that would only yeild a potential minimal improvement to data timelyness.
I've tested with the changes and it appears to be working as intended.

review_comments: I saw your message on Discord. This will indeed log an error everytime it loses connectivity. Another solution would be to return `dict[str, Any] | None` here and have all entities handle getting no data. They can turn unknown or unavailable (I think I prefer unknown as you don't know the state).
Unknown makes more sense, I agree.
The problem with setting all states to None is I'd have no way to restore them if the car is asleep when it reconnects. I also think unavailable is the correct state for temporary connectivity loss.
